messages.subject: User defined GWAS model
parts:
Hi all,

I am just trying to run the user defined GWAS model, using the following command:
modelGWAS<-userGWAS(SNPcov,estimation="DWLS", model=CommonFactor_userDefined)

For some reason I keep getting this error:
"Error in lavInspect(ReorderModel1, "cor.lv") :
  object 'ReorderModel1' not found"

I don't think it has something to do with model misspecificaton, as I have been able to test the same user defined model including only the output from LD-Score regression, which ran find and showed good model fit statistics:

    chisq df      p_chisq      AIC       CFI      SRMR
df 32.04187 11 0.0007510184 66.04187 0.9599586 0.1131122

Any idea what I am doing wrong here?

As always, many thanks for your help,

Tabea

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: User defined GWAS model
parts:
Hi Tabea, 

It's strange that you are able to run the model without the individual SNP-effect without issue, but typically I've seen this error pop up when the model is not identified in some way. Is it possible for you to paste the CommonFactor_userDefined model here so I can take a look at the model you are running? I know a specific model identification issues others have run into when running a  common factor model using userGWAS is using unit loading identification for a variable that does not load very highly on the common factor. So in the case of the p-factor model we show on the wiki if I write the code below, then lavaan will fix the loading of anxiety to 1, but since anxiety does not load as highly on the p-factor then the scaling for the other common factor indicators is difficult for lavaan to deal with. On the off chance this is the issue you are running into, this can be solved by listing the variable that loads the highest on the common factor first. 

pfactor.model<-'F1=~ANX + SCZ + MDD + PTSD + BIP
F1~SNP'

Hi Arianna, 

Glad you got it working! If you are running the script in parallel (which is the package default unless you set parallel = FALSE) then it won't print updates as of right now (something I'm hoping to add in for the coming weeks because I know it can be unclear if it's just spinning its wheels or actually making progress). I would suggest running a subset of 5k or so SNPs just to get a sense of overall run time and to make sure it isn't running into any issues. Also just a note to say that if you are running on a cluster, I also recommend splitting the summary stats file in batches to run separate jobs just to speed things up. If you are running in serial it will print updates for every 1k SNPs it runs. 

Best,
-Andrew

messages.subject: Re: User defined GWAS model
parts:
This is just a note to say that Arianna reached out over e-mail with a separate error she was getting: 
"Error in lav_fit_measures(object = object, fit.measures = fit.measures,  :
  lavaan ERROR: fit measures not available if model did not converge" 

The issue was that a model lavaan internally uses to estimate model fit was crashing for a subset of your SNPs, and this was causing the function to break at a later point. This is ultimately not an issue with the model, because Genomic SEM does not use lavaan model fit indices, but had been using the "fit" function from lavaan to pull out degrees of freedom and free parameters, which was throwing the error. I've updated the GWAS functions to pull out degrees of freedom and number of free parameters independent of that function so anyone who runs into this error should make sure that they are using the most recent version of Genomic SEM.

messages.author: 0b5254eeb9973d7a
messages.subject: Re: User defined GWAS model
parts:
Dear Moreh,

I would recommend against using the word "causal" unless you are referring to something like Mendelian Randomization. I take it that you are referring to whether you can specify a model that includes paths from the SNP to all GWAS phenotypes. That is straightforward to do using the standard lavaan syntax. Keep in mind that you typically can't have a model that estimates paths from the SNPs to all indicators of a factor and additionally estimates paths to the factor. Such a model is typically underidentified.

Also note that the Q statistic for the common factor GWAS compares a model with a path from the SNP to the factor to a model with paths from the SNP to all indicators (but not the factor). This is described in the original Grotzinger at all paper in Nature Human Behaviour, and further discussed in the supplement to the forthcoming de la Fuente paper (see section "Interpreting the Heterogeneity Statistic" and Figure S9). Papers below:

de la Fuente, J., Davies, J., Grotzinger, A. D., Tucker-Drob, E. M., & Deary. (in press). A general dimension of genetic sharing across diverse cognitive traits inferred from molecular data. Nature Human Behaviour. [de la Fuente & Davies contributed equally to this work; Tucker-Drob & Deary jointly directed this work] Link (to preprint)

Grotzinger, A. D., Rhemtulla, M., de Vlaming, R., Ritchie, S. J., Mallard, T. T.,  Hill, W. D, Ip, H. F., Marioni, R. E., McIntosh, A. M., Deary, I. J., Koellinger, P. D., Harden, K. P., Nivard, M. G., & Tucker-Drob, E. M. (2019). Genomic structural equation modelling provides insights into the multivariate genetic architecture of complex traits. Nature Human Behaviour, 3, 513-525. [Nivard & Tucker-Drob jointly directed this work] Paper Supplement(Text/Figures) Supplement(Tables) 

Cheers,

Elliot

On Thursday, August 6, 2020 at 2:08:02 PM UTC+1, Elliot Tucker-Drob wrote:

Dear Moreh,

I would recommend against using the word "causal" unless you are referring to something like Mendelian Randomization. I take it that you are referring to whether you can specify a model that includes paths from the SNP to all GWAS phenotypes. That is straightforward to do using the standard lavaan syntax. Keep in mind that you typically can't have a model that estimates paths from the SNPs to all indicators of a factor and additionally estimates paths to the factor. Such a model is typically underidentified.

Also note that the Q statistic for the common factor GWAS compares a model with a path from the SNP to the factor to a model with paths from the SNP to all indicators (but not the factor). This is described in the original Grotzinger at all paper in Nature Human Behaviour, and further discussed in the supplement to the forthcoming de la Fuente paper (see section "Interpreting the Heterogeneity Statistic" and Figure S9). Papers below:

de la Fuente, J., Davies, J., Grotzinger, A. D., Tucker-Drob, E. M., & Deary. (in press). A general dimension of genetic sharing across diverse cognitive traits inferred from molecular data. Nature Human Behaviour. [de la Fuente & Davies contributed equally to this work; Tucker-Drob & Deary jointly directed this work] Link (to preprint)

Grotzinger, A. D., Rhemtulla, M., de Vlaming, R., Ritchie, S. J., Mallard, T. T.,  Hill, W. D, Ip, H. F., Marioni, R. E., McIntosh, A. M., Deary, I. J., Koellinger, P. D., Harden, K. P., Nivard, M. G., & Tucker-Drob, E. M. (2019). Genomic structural equation modelling provides insights into the multivariate genetic architecture of complex traits. Nature Human Behaviour, 3, 513-525. [Nivard & Tucker-Drob jointly directed this work] Paper Supplement(Text/Figures) Supplement(Tables) 

Cheers,

Elliot
